options.A: Each user's TPOT stays exactly the same until compute runs out, and throughput rises 64 times
options.B: Total tokens per second rise a lot, each user's TPOT rises a little, and KV memory caps how many users fit
options.C: Both total throughput and each user's TPOT improve, since the GPU is busier and works more efficiently per token
options.D: Total throughput stays the same, since the GPU is already busy; each user just gets 64 times slower

options.A: Training uses a KV cache to skip recomputation
options.B: One failed GPU stalls a whole synchronized training job, so teams checkpoint often
options.C: Training needs several times the memory per parameter (gradients and optimizer state)
options.D: Training GPUs must exchange gradients every step, so the network and stragglers matter as much as the chips
options.E: Serving updates the weights after every request

options.A: Nothing: training would crash, because softmax needs at least one masked score in every row
options.B: To copy the next token from the input, since it could see it; at generation that token doesn't exist yet
options.C: To generate whole sentences at once, since every position would see every other one at the same time
options.D: Exactly the same thing, only slower, since each position would also attend to positions it then ignores

options.A: A dead-letter queue: future tokens are parked to one side and processed after the current one finishes
options.B: A load balancer: each token is routed only to the attention heads that are free
options.C: A snapshot read: each transaction sees only what committed before it, never later writes
options.D: Rate limiting: each token may only attend to a fixed number of others per step

options.A: Decode is memory-bound, so fewer weight bytes speed it up; prefill is compute-bound, so smaller weights barely help
options.B: Prefill doesn't read the weights at all; it only builds the KV cache from the prompt's embeddings
options.C: Prefill results are already cached from earlier requests, so there is little left for it to speed up
options.D: Quantization only shrinks the output layer, which decode runs on every step but prefill runs only once per prompt

options.A: 1 − p can go negative when the model is very confident, which would reward a wrong answer instead of punishing it
options.B: There is no difference in what the model learns: both are lowest at p = 1, so −ln p is just convention
options.C: −ln p is cheaper to compute on a GPU than a subtraction across the whole vocabulary
options.D: −ln p grows without limit as p → 0, so confident wrong answers are punished hard; 1 − p caps the penalty at 1

options.A: Return an error, since the prompt lacks the chat template a base model expects
options.B: Answer politely like a chat assistant, since question-and-answer text is all over its training data
options.C: Refuse, because a base model has no instructions telling it how to respond to users
options.D: Continue the text as a document would, perhaps with more quiz questions, rather than answer

options.A: The answer gets more accurate
options.B: TPOT: each output token gets much faster
options.C: TTFT: only the new tokens need prefill
options.D: Input cost: providers bill cached input tokens at a discount

options.A: Adding GPUs (tensor parallelism): more bandwidth per tick and more room for caches
options.B: Raising the batch size: more users share each weight read, so each user's TPOT drops
options.C: Quantizing to 8-bit: half the bytes per tick and room for twice the caches
options.D: Lowering the temperature: fewer candidate tokens per step, so each tick is faster

options.A: Adds a second, smaller model that tracks the conversation and hands the main model one turn at a time
options.B: Rewrites the user's prompt into a fixed question format, the one the base model saw most in pre-training
options.C: Stores past conversations on the server so the model can recall them in a later session
options.D: Wraps each turn in special tokens like <|user|> and flattens the messages into one string to continue

options.A: Quantized weights, so each tick reads fewer bytes
options.B: Higher temperature
options.C: Smaller KV caches (shorter contexts, fewer KV heads), so more users fit in a batch
options.D: Longer contexts per request
options.E: Larger decode batches, so each weight read is shared by more users

options.A: A new answer-generation layer is added on top of the base model, and only that layer is trained on dialogue
options.B: The next-token loss is replaced by a reward score, so the model learns what people prefer
options.C: Only the weight values, via more training with the same next-token loss on curated prompt → answer pairs
options.D: The tokenizer is retrained for dialogue, so turns and roles get pieces of their own

options.A: More tokens per second while busy (batching, quantization, better kernels)
options.B: A bigger vocabulary
options.C: Lower temperature
options.D: A higher busy share of each paid hour (traffic, autoscaling, sharing GPUs across models)

options.A: The number of tokens at which the chosen and rejected answers differ from each other
options.B: The reward model's score for the chosen answer minus its score for the rejected one, as in RLHF
options.C: How much more the model now favors chosen over rejected, compared with the starting model
options.D: The difference in length between the chosen and rejected answers, which DPO penalizes

options.A: The text supplies the answer: the right label at each position is simply the next token
options.B: It does need labels; they are crowdsourced, which is why pre-training costs so much
options.C: Labels are added later during fine-tuning; pre-training only learns word statistics
options.D: A smaller model labels the text first, and the large model then learns from those labels

options.A: Temperature can drop and sampling can be skipped, since 8-bit logits are already sharp
options.B: The model needs fewer layers and a smaller vocabulary, so each decode tick has less work to do in total
options.C: Each tick reads half the weight bytes, and the freed memory holds more KV caches for a bigger batch
options.D: Prompts and answers get shorter, since 8-bit weights produce more compact tokens

options.A: Fixed content first (system prompt, tools, examples); changing content (user message, time) last
options.B: Put a timestamp at the top so the cache can tell how old the prompt is and expire it in time
options.C: Order doesn't matter; the cache matches any shared stretch of text wherever it appears in the prompt
options.D: User message first, so it gets the most attention, then the system prompt and tools after it

options.A: A CDN edge cache: answers to common prompts are stored near users and served without running the model
options.B: A circuit breaker: requests beyond the batch size are rejected until the GPU recovers
options.C: Group commit: many transactions share one disk flush, so each waits a bit longer but throughput rises
options.D: Read replicas: each user in the batch gets a copy of the weights to read from in parallel

options.A: Output tokens are longer than input tokens, because the model writes whole words rather than pieces
options.B: Input tokens share each weight read in prefill; each output step reads all the weights to emit one token per user
options.C: Providers charge more for output to discourage long answers; the GPU time per token is actually about the same
options.D: Output tokens pass through more layers than input tokens, since the model must also pick the next token

options.A: Add −∞ to scores above the diagonal before softmax, so future positions get exactly 0 weight
options.B: Multiply the values of future tokens by 0.5, so they count for half in the weighted average
options.C: Delete the future tokens from the input, so each position runs on a shorter sequence
options.D: Set the attention weights above the diagonal to 0 after the weighted average has been taken

options.A: The mask makes each position see only itself and earlier positions, exactly as during generation
options.B: They don't match exactly; a short extra training phase adjusts the model so generation roughly agrees
options.C: Both run at the same temperature, so the probabilities they compute come out identical
options.D: Generation quietly retrains the model after each token so it stays in step with training

options.A: SFT examples teach facts far more efficiently than pre-training tokens, so most knowledge comes from SFT
options.B: SFT overwrites most of what pre-training learned, so a small set is enough to rebuild it
options.C: Knowledge comes from pre-training; a small, high-quality SFT set mainly shapes behavior and format
options.D: Pre-training is mostly wasted, since the useful skills only appear once SFT begins

options.A: A message queue: prompts wait until enough with the same prefix arrive to process them together
options.B: Database sharding: each prefix is pinned to one server, which keeps its cache forever
options.C: A write-through cache in front of a database: every new prompt is written to the cache and to disk
options.D: A content-addressed cache with a TTL: hash prefix blocks, look them up, expire after minutes

options.A: The causal mask would stop working, because the prompt tokens would then be able to see the answer after them
options.B: The model would forget its vocabulary, since prompt tokens would dominate every gradient step
options.C: Effort would go into predicting user messages, so the model learns to write prompts as well as answers
options.D: Nothing much; scoring the prompt only costs a little more compute per training example

options.A: The server re-checks every stored value against the new request and recomputes any that differ
options.B: It isn't fully safe; small errors from a different request's context are accepted for the speed
options.C: Keys and values at position i depend only on tokens 1…i, so an identical prefix always gives identical KV
options.D: KV values come from the weights alone, so they are the same for every prompt and any stored copy works for any request

options.A: Throughput: total tokens per second across all users
options.B: Time to compute the KV cache size
options.C: End-to-end latency: the time until the whole answer has finished
options.D: TTFT (time to first token): how long before anything appears

options.A: RLHF: a reward model and reinforcement learning, generating during training. DPO: one loss on chosen/rejected pairs
options.B: RLHF trains on single answers rated by people; DPO needs whole conversations, with every turn scored by people
options.C: Both need a trained reward model and sampled answers during training; DPO just trains its reward model faster
options.D: RLHF: only human-written answers, trained like SFT. DPO: a reward model scoring the model's own answers

options.A: −ln p for the correct token, and 0 for every other token
options.B: p − 1 for the correct token, and p for every other token
options.C: p for the correct token, and p − 1 for every other token
